x.ASV: A Song of Ascents. Jehovah, remember for David All his affliction;
x.Darby: A Song of degrees. Jehovah, remember for David all his affliction;
x.KJV: A Song of degrees. Lord, remember David, and all his afflictions:
x.YLT: A Song of the Ascents. Remember, Jehovah, for David, all his afflictions.

nt: This is an imperative, but it communicates a polite request rather than a command. The psalmist is praying to God. If the imperative does not communicate a polite request for your readers, then use a form in your language that communicates a polite request. It may be helpful to add an expression such as “please” to make this clear. Alternate translation: [Please remember, Yahweh]
The pronoun **his** refers to David. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [all of David’s afflictions]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **afflictions**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [the hardships he endured]

x.ASV: How he sware unto Jehovah, And vowed unto the Mighty One of Jacob:
x.Darby: How he swore unto Jehovah, vowed unto the Mighty One of Jacob:
x.KJV: How he sware unto the Lord, and vowed unto the mighty God of Jacob;
x.YLT: Who hath sworn to Jehovah. He hath vowed to the Mighty One of Jacob:

nt: אֲשֶׁ֣ר נִ֭שְׁבַּע לַ⁠יהוָ֑ה נָ֝דַ֗ר לַ⁠אֲבִ֥יר יַעֲקֹֽב

These two phrases mean basically the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could combine them and express the emphasis in another way, as the UST does. Another approach would be to connect the phrases with a word that shows that the second phrase is repeating the first one, not saying something additional. See how you as a team have decided to translate the parallel phrases in the Psalms, and follow that approach here and throughout this psalm. Alternate translation: [who swore to Yahweh, yes, he vowed to the Mighty One of Jacob]

If it would be helpful to your readers, you could mark the end of this verse in a way that shows that the next verse is the beginning of David’s oath. Alternate translation: [vowed to the Mighty One of Jacob, saying,]

x.ASV: Surely I will not come into the tabernacle of my house, Nor go up into my bed;
x.Darby: I will not come into the tent of my house, I will not go up to the couch of my bed;
x.KJV: Surely I will not come into the tabernacle of my house, nor go up into my bed;
x.YLT: `If I enter into the tent of my house, If I go up on the couch of my bed,

nt: אִם־אָ֭בֹא בְּ⁠אֹ֣הֶל בֵּיתִ֑⁠י אִם־אֶ֝עֱלֶ֗ה עַל־עֶ֥רֶשׂ יְצוּעָֽ⁠י

Following the custom of the culture, David is swearing an oath by stating several conditions (“if”) from this verse through verse 5, but not the consequences for not meeting those conditions (“then”). The implied meaning is that something bad will happen to him if he does these things before finding a place for Yahweh.

x.ASV: I will not give sleep to mine eyes, Or slumber to mine eyelids;
x.Darby: I will not give sleep to mine eyes, slumber to mine eyelids,
x.KJV: I will not give sleep to mine eyes, or slumber to mine eyelids,
x.YLT: If I give sleep to mine eyes, To mine eyelids--slumber,

nt: The psalmist is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [if I give slumber to my eyelids]

x.ASV: Until I find out a place for Jehovah, A tabernacle for the Mighty One of Jacob.
x.Darby: Until I find out a place for Jehovah, habitations for the Mighty One of Jacob....
x.KJV: Until I find out a place for the Lord, an habitation for the mighty God of Jacob.
x.YLT: Till I do find a place for Jehovah, Tabernacles for the Mighty One of Jacob.

nt: עַד־אֶמְצָ֣א מָ֭קוֹם לַ⁠יהוָ֑ה מִ֝שְׁכָּנ֗וֹת לַ⁠אֲבִ֥יר יַעֲקֹֽב

Following the custom of the culture, the psalmist is quoting David as swearing an oath by stating the first part of a condition (“if” clauses in verses 3 and 4) but not the second part (“then”). If it would be helpful to your readers, you could explicitly state the consequence of not meeting this condition. Alternate translation: [until I find a place for Yahweh, dwellings for the Mighty One of Jacob, then may God strike me down]

The psalmist is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [until I find dwellings for the Mighty One of Jacob]

x.ASV: Lo, we heard of it in Ephrathah: We found it in the field of the wood.
x.Darby: Behold, we heard of it at Ephratah, we found it in the fields of the wood.
x.KJV: Lo, we heard of it at Ephratah: we found it in the fields of the wood.
x.YLT: `Lo, we have heard it in Ephratah, We have found it in the fields of the forest.

nt: The psalmist is using the term **behold** to focus his listeners’ attention on what he is about to say. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation. Alternate translation: [Pay attention]

The pronoun **it** in both clauses refers to the ark of the covenant. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [we heard of the ark of the covenant in Ephrathah; we found the ark in the fields of Jaar]

x.ASV: We will go into his tabernacles; We will worship at his footstool.
x.Darby: Let us go into his habitations, let us worship at his footstool.
x.KJV: We will go into his tabernacles: we will worship at his footstool.
x.YLT: We come in to His tabernacles, We bow ourselves at His footstool.

nt: This is the beginning of what the community of worshipers said. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could mark that this is a direct quote of the community. Alternate translation: [We said to one another, “Let us go to his dwellings]
The pronoun **his** refers to Yahweh. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [Yahweh’s dwellings]

Here, **bow down** is describing a symbolic action by which people showed reverence and submission as an act of worship. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could explain the significance of this action in the text of your translation. Alternate translation: [let us bow down in worship]

Here the psalmist is speaking of the ark of the covenant as if it were **the footstool of his feet**, that is, the place where Yahweh rests his feet as he sits enthroned above the cherubs. You may have a comparable expression in your language, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [the place where he rests his feet]

x.ASV: Arise, O Jehovah, into thy resting-place; Thou, and the ark of thy strength.
x.Darby: Arise, Jehovah, into thy rest, thou and the ark of thy strength.
x.KJV: Arise, O Lord, into thy rest; thou, and the ark of thy strength.
x.YLT: Arise, O Jehovah, to Thy rest, Thou, and the ark of Thy strength,

nt: This is an imperative, but it communicates a polite request rather than a command. The psalmist is praying to God. If the imperative does not communicate a polite request for your readers, then use a form in your language that communicates a polite request. It may be helpful to add an expression such as “please” to make this clear. Alternate translation: [Please arise, Yahweh]

The psalmist is using **Arise** as a common expression of the culture to tell Yahweh to take action and come to his resting place. He is not telling Yahweh to stand up from a seated position. If this expression does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly as modeled in the UST.

Here Yahweh is speaking of remaining in one place as if he were **resting** there. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [come where you can remain]

Here, **strength** represents Yahweh’s powerful presence. The box (ark of the covenant) is called the box of Yahweh’s strength because it symbolized his powerful presence among the people. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [and the box where your power resides]

x.ASV: Let thy priests be clothed with righteousness; And let thy saints shout for joy.
x.Darby: Let thy priests be clothed with righteousness, and let thy saints shout for joy.
x.KJV: Let thy priests be clothed with righteousness; and let thy saints shout for joy.
x.YLT: Thy priests do put on righteousness, And Thy pious ones cry aloud.

nt: The psalmist is saying what he wants the priests and the faithful ones to do. See the discussion in the introduction to this book about “let” and “may” and follow the decision of your team of how a speaker will express in this context what he wants someone to do. Alternate translation: [Your priests should wear righteousness and your faithful ones should shout for joy]

Here the psalmist is speaking of **righteousness** as if it were clothing that the priests could **wear**. He means that the priests should be characterized by righteous behavior. If this image communicates well in your language, please use it. If not, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Let your priests be righteous in all they do]

If your language does not use abstract nouns for the ideas of **righteousness** and **joy**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [righteous acts and let your faithful shout joyfully]

The psalmist is using the adjective **faithful** as a noun to mean people who are faithful to God. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate this adjective with an equivalent phrase. Alternate translation: [and your faithful people should shout for joy]

x.ASV: For thy servant David’s sake Turn not away the face of thine anointed.
x.Darby: For thy servant David's sake, turn not away the face of thine anointed.
x.KJV: For thy servant David’s sake turn not away the face of thine anointed.
x.YLT: For the sake of David Thy servant, Turn not back the face of Thine anointed.

nt: This is an imperative, but it communicates a polite request rather than a command. The psalmist is asking God not to reject the anointed king. If the imperative does not communicate a polite request for your readers, then use a form in your language that communicates a polite request. It may be helpful to add an expression such as “please” to make this clear. Alternate translation: [please do not turn back the face of your anointed]

The psalmist is using **turn back the face** as a common expression of his culture to mean “reject.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [reject]

x.ASV: Jehovah hath sworn unto David in truth; He will not turn from it: Of the fruit of thy body will I set upon thy throne.
x.Darby: Jehovah hath sworn [in] truth unto David; he will not turn from it: Of the fruit of thy body will I set upon thy throne;
x.KJV: The Lord hath sworn in truth unto David; he will not turn from it; Of the fruit of thy body will I set upon thy throne.
x.YLT: Jehovah hath sworn truth to David, He turneth not back from it: Of the fruit of thy body, I set on the throne for thee.

nt: If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **truth**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [surely]

The pronoun **he** refers to Yahweh, and the pronoun **it** refers to the oath that he swore. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [Yahweh will not turn back from his promise]

Here the psalmist is speaking of Yahweh changing his mind about his promise as if he were going one way and then decided to **turn back from it**. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [he will not change his mind about it]

After the clause “he will not turn back from it,” Yahweh’s direct speech begins. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could mark that this is a direct quote of Yahweh. Alternate translation: [Yahweh said, “From the fruit of your body]

Here Yahweh is speaking of David’s children as if they were **the fruit** that his body produces. If this image communicates well in your language, please use it. If not, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [From among your offspring]

Here Yahweh is speaking of choosing one of David’s sons to rule his kingdom after him as if he were going to physically **set** him **on the throne**. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [I will cause one of your sons to rule over Israel after you]

Here, **the throne** represents royal authority and the right to rule as king. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [as king over your kingdom]

x.ASV: If thy children will keep my covenant And my testimony that I shall teach them, Their children also shall sit upon thy throne for evermore.
x.Darby: If thy children keep my covenant, and my testimonies which I will teach them, their children also for evermore shall sit upon thy throne.
x.KJV: If thy children will keep my covenant and my testimony that I shall teach them, their children shall also sit upon thy throne for evermore.
x.YLT: If thy sons keep My covenant, And My testimonies that I teach them, Their sons also for ever and ever, Do sit on the throne for thee.

nt: The terms **covenant** and **testimonies** mean similar things. Yahweh is using the two terms together for emphasis. If it would be clearer for your readers, you could express the emphasis with a single phrase. Alternate translation: [all my commands]

Here, **sit on the throne** represents ruling as king. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [will succeed you as kings]

x.ASV: For Jehovah hath chosen Zion; He hath desired it for his habitation.
x.Darby: For Jehovah hath chosen Zion; he hath desired it for his dwelling:
x.KJV: For the Lord hath chosen Zion; he hath desired it for his habitation.
x.YLT: For Jehovah hath fixed on Zion, He hath desired it for a seat to Himself,

nt: Here the word **For** introduces not a reason but an explanation. You may want to use a different connecting word to show how this statement relates to what comes before it. Alternate translation: [Certainly,]

x.ASV: This is my resting-place for ever: Here will I dwell; for I have desired it.
x.Darby: This is my rest for ever; here will I dwell, for I have desired it.
x.KJV: This is my rest for ever: here will I dwell; for I have desired it.
x.YLT: This is My rest for ever and ever, Here do I sit, for I have desired it.

nt: This is the beginning of what Yahweh said. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could mark that this is a direct quote of Yahweh. Alternate translation: [Yahweh said, “This is my resting place]

Here Yahweh is speaking of remaining in one place as if he were **resting** there. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [where I will remain]

The word **for** here indicates that what follows is a reason for Yahweh’s decision to dwell in Zion. Use a connector in your language that makes it clear that what follows is a reason for what came before. Alternate translation: [because I have desired it]

x.ASV: I will abundantly bless her provision: I will satisfy her poor with bread.
x.Darby: I will abundantly bless her provision; I will satisfy her needy ones with bread;
x.KJV: I will abundantly bless her provision: I will satisfy her poor with bread.
x.YLT: Her provision I greatly bless, Her needy ones I satisfy with bread,

nt: Yahweh is repeating forms of the verb **bless** in order to intensify his expression of the idea that it conveys. If your language can repeat words for intensification, it would be appropriate to do that here in your translation. If not, your language may have another way of expressing the intensification. Alternate translation: [I will abundantly bless]
Here and through the next verse, the pronoun **her** refers to Zion (see [verse 13](../132/013.md)). It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [Zion’s provisions]

Yahweh is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [I will bless her needy]

Yahweh is using the adjective **needy** as a noun to mean people who are in need. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate this adjective with an equivalent phrase. Alternate translation: [her needy people]
The psalmist is using one kind of food, **bread**, to mean food in general. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use a general expression. Alternate translation: [with enough to eat]

x.ASV: Her priests also will I clothe with salvation; And her saints shall shout aloud for joy.
x.Darby: And I will clothe her priests with salvation, and her saints shall shout aloud for joy.
x.KJV: I will also clothe her priests with salvation: and her saints shall shout aloud for joy.
x.YLT: And her priests I clothe with salvation, And her pious ones do sing aloud.

nt: Here Yahweh is speaking the priests being examples of his saving power as if **salvation** were clothing that the priests could wear. If this image communicates well in your language, please use it. If not, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [And her priests I will make examples of my saving power]

If your language does not use an abstract nouns for the ideas of **salvation** and **joy**, you could express the same ideas in another way. Alternate translation: [with the evidence that I save people, and her faithful people will shout joyfully]

Yahweh is using the adjective **faithful** as a noun to mean people who are faithful to God. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate this adjective with an equivalent phrase. Alternate translation: [and her faithful people]

Yahweh is repeating forms of the verb **shout** in order to intensify his expression of the idea that it conveys. If your language can repeat words for intensification, it would be appropriate to do that here in your translation. If not, your language may have another way of expressing the intensification. Alternate translation: [they will shout loudly for joy]

x.ASV: There will I make the horn of David to bud: I have ordained a lamp for mine anointed.
x.Darby: There will I cause the horn of David to bud forth; I have ordained a lamp for mine anointed.
x.KJV: There will I make the horn of David to bud: I have ordained a lamp for mine anointed.
x.YLT: There I cause to spring up a horn for David, I have arranged a lamp for Mine anointed.

nt: The word **There** refers to Zion, which was mentioned in verse 13. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [There in Zion]

Here Yahweh is speaking of son of David’s being born who will be powerful as if he were a **horn** that would **sprout** like a plant growing. A horn represents strength and power, and sprouting represents the arising of something new. If this image communicates well in your language, please use it. If not, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [I will make a powerful king rise up from David’s line]

Here Yahweh is speaking of the continuing dynasty of the anointed king as if it were **a lamp** that keeps burning. A lamp that stays lit represents the continuation of a family line or kingdom. If this image communicates well in your language, please use it. If not, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [a continuing dynasty for my anointed one]

x.ASV: His enemies will I clothe with shame; But upon himself shall his crown flourish.
x.Darby: His enemies will I clothe with shame; but upon himself shall his crown flourish.
x.KJV: His enemies will I clothe with shame: but upon himself shall his crown flourish.
x.YLT: His enemies I do clothe with shame, And upon him doth his crown flourish!

nt: Here Yahweh is speaking of **shame** as if the enemies would wear it like clothing. If this image communicates well in your language, please use it. If not, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [His enemies I will thoroughly put to shame]

Here, **His** and the pronoun **him** later in the verse refer to the anointed one mentioned in the previous verse. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [The anointed one’s enemies]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **shame**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [I will shame]

Yahweh uses the word **but** here to indicate a contrast between the fate of the anointed one’s enemies and the fate of the anointed one himself. In your translation, indicate this contrast in a way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [however, upon him his crown will flourish]

Here Yahweh is speaking of the anointed one’s crown as if it were a plant that would **flourish** and grow. He means that the anointed one’s reign will prosper and thrive. If this image communicates well in your language, please use it. If not, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [his reign will be successful]
